sections.html:
Charleston grew up around its harbor, fed by three rivers (the Ashley, the Cooper and the Wando). It has more residents than any other South Carolina city and serves as county seat for Charleston County. Residents numbered 150,227 in 2020, against 120,083 a decade earlier, and the latest estimate is 159,423. Total area is 135.51 square miles, of which 115.03 is land.

One wrinkle: the city limits straddle two counties, Charleston and Berkeley. Whichever county holds your parcel supplies your assessor and treasurer, so read the name on your tax bill before dialing. The neighborhoods also vary a great deal: the downtown peninsula, West Ashley, Johns Island, James Island, the Cainhoy Peninsula and Daniel Island each carry different flood exposure, parking rules and rental rules.

Almost every Charleston sale involves a flood conversation. Elevation averages about 3 feet, and the city names the Stono, Ashley, Cooper and Wando, a string of creeks and the ocean as sources of flooding. A lot outside the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area can still suffer from local drainage trouble, unmapped floodplain or rising seas. The city's 2019 Flooding and Sea Level Rise Strategy advises planning for 2.0 to 3.0 feet of sea level rise over the next 50 years.

The city issues a Flood Hazard Information Letter that shows a property's flood zone. Send requests for elevation certificates and flood details to floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov. If you think the FEMA map is wrong, for example because the lot sits above the Base Flood Elevation or was filled, you can file a Letter of Map Change with FEMA. An elevation certificate sent along with a map request can be flagged for problems such as inadequate flood openings in a garage enclosure, so have it checked first. The city's Floodplain Mapping page explains the process.

Before listing, pull together the roof's age, repair invoices and a note of any past water damage. Storm history is a standard buyer question here.

sections.h2: Who bills the tax and when it is due
sections.html:
Valuation belongs to the Charleston County Assessor, and billing and collection belong to the Charleston County Treasurer. Real estate tax is due January 15 of the following year without penalty, and a U.S. postmark decides whether a mailed payment was on time (S.C. Code 12-45-180).

StepPenaltyRunning total
After January 153%3%
After February 1Additional 7%10%
After March 17Additional 5%, then to Delinquent Tax15%

Partial payments are refused, since state law does not permit them, and paying online adds a surcharge. Visit the Treasurer at 101 Meeting St., Suite 120, Charleston, SC 29401, phone (843) 958-4360. For how an unpaid balance is handled at closing, ask the Treasurer or your title company. After a refinance, forward the bill to the new lender so escrow covers it.

The state works on a five-year reassessment cycle. Charleston County's newest notices went out August 20, 2025. The Assessor appraises about 190,000 real property parcels and 6,500 titled mobile homes.

When market value rises by more than 15%, the increase in taxable value is capped at 15% over the earlier figure. The cap limits value, not the bill, since millage can change. Newly added property, property with 2024 construction and property with a 2024 Assessable Transfer of Interest may be uncapped or only partly capped.

  • Any appeal has to be written, signed by hand and addressed to the Assessor.
  • The objection window is 90 days after notices are mailed.
  • If no notice was sent that year, the appeal period generally closes on the tax due date, typically January 15.
  • Later stages carry 30-day deadlines, and filing an appeal does not delay the bill.

Phone, email and fax do not protect your rights. The Assessor's office is at 4050 Bridge View Dr., Suite 100, North Charleston, SC 29405, phone (843) 958-4100.

sections.h2: The 4% rate and what happens when the owner moves
sections.html:
Homes lived in by their owners are taxed at 4% of fair market value, and all other real property at 6%. Nothing about the 4% rate is automatic. Under S.C. Code 12-43-220, the owner must own and occupy the home as a legal residence and be domiciled there. Properties without approval are billed at 6%, and a bill shows "QR4" when the 4% rate is in place. The application deadline is typically January 15.

The statute also bars renting the home for more than 72 days in a calendar year. An owner who loses eligibility has six months to tell the assessor, or faces a penalty of 100% of the tax paid plus interest.

Sellers who moved out before listing should take note. If the house was rented out or left empty, the 6% rate can apply, and the figure needed at closing may surprise you.

Charleston sorts short-term rentals into three categories, with a ceiling of one STR unit on any property. Category 1 is the Old and Historic District. Category 2 is the rest of the peninsula. Category 3 covers Daniel Island, James Island, Johns Island and West Ashley.

  • All three require a further off-street parking space, on top of the two that zoning demands for each dwelling unit.
  • Category 1 needs a structure individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
  • Category 2 needs a building constructed at least 50 years ago.

The city points owners to its property eligibility quiz or shorttermrental@charleston-sc.gov (city category page). If you are marketing a house with rental income, get the permit status confirmed in writing, since the rules depend on location.

Owing tax does not block a Charleston sale. Closing usually pays the debt from your proceeds. Get the payoff from the Treasurer before signing a contract, as the figure jumps on February 1 and again on March 17.

Overpaid tax can be refunded on request for up to two years back, which helps a seller who was charged 6% while qualified for 4%. Keep copies of every notice and receipt so the Assessor can trace the years involved. A title company can often spot a rate mix-up in the payoff before it reaches your closing table.

  1. Ask the Treasurer's Office for the payoff.
  2. Confirm the legal residence status with the Assessor.
  3. Order the Flood Hazard Information Letter so the buyer can see the zone.
  4. Confirm with the Assessor that the address on the bill matches the address you will list under.
  5. Verify the short-term rental permit if rental income is part of your listing.

faqs.q: When is Charleston County property tax due?
faqs.a: The last penalty-free day is January 15 of the following year. After it come 3%, then another 7% after February 1 and another 5% after March 17.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Charleston assessment?
faqs.a: Ninety days from the mailing of the notice, in a signed written objection sent to the Assessor. A phone call, email or fax will not protect your rights.

faqs.q: Is Charleston in more than one county?
faqs.a: Yes, the city reaches into both Charleston and Berkeley counties. The tax bill names the county that serves your parcel.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Charleston house if I owe back property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing normally pays the back tax out of your proceeds. Request a payoff from the Treasurer first, since the 10% and 15% totals kick in after February 1 and March 17.

faqs.q: Does Charleston have a flood-zone disclosure tool?
faqs.a: Yes. The city provides a Flood Hazard Information Letter that lists the flood zone for a property. Contact floodplain-info@charleston-sc.gov for elevation certificates.
